title: Collapse and seizure at a construction site on a humid morning

source.citation: Ikeda T, Watase T, Kondo T, Watase H, Funabiki T, Iwata M. Low-volume body bag cooling for severe exertional heat stroke in the emergency department: a case report. Int J Emerg Med. 2026;19(1):274.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Collapsed with seizure-like activity at a construction site
presentation.hpi: Seven months after umbilical cord blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukemia, he returned to outdoor work yesterday without heat acclimatization. This morning, after 90 minutes of pipe-cutting at an ambient 36 °C and 65% humidity, he became dizzy and collapsed with witnessed seizure-like activity. EMS arrived within 26 minutes and started 500 mL of cold IV fluid. During transport: GCS 3, BP 72/49 mm Hg, HR 155/min, RR 30/min, axillary temperature 42.0 °C.
pmh: Acute myeloid leukemia, status post umbilical cord blood transplantation 7 months ago
presentation.social: Construction worker; returned to outdoor work the day before without heat acclimatization.

investigations.name: Blood cultures
investigations.value: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus caprae; no source identified

ecg: Continuous monitoring through defibrillator pads during cooling: no arrhythmia

diagnosis.primary: Exertional heat stroke (rectal temperature 42.0 °C with coma) complicated by rhabdomyolysis and hepatic injury, in an unacclimatized, immunosuppressed outdoor worker

management: EMS: 500 mL of cold IV fluid during transport

Body bag tarp-assisted cooling with oscillation (TACO) started on arrival: 15 L tap water plus 15 kg ice prepared in advance, about half the body immersed, the bag agitated continuously from its four corners; ice packs to axillae and groins
Endotracheal intubation (ketamine, rocuronium) for airway protection while immersed, without interrupting cooling
Monitoring with defibrillator pads, ear-lobe pulse oximetry, intermittent arm blood pressure, continuous bladder and intermittent rectal temperatures
Cold acetated Ringer's solution, 2,500 mL during the ED stay
Cooling stopped after 39 minutes at a rectal temperature of 38.7 °C (0.085 °C/min); the bag was drained by cutting one corner
ICU admission; transferred out of the ICU on hospital day 5; prolonged antimicrobial therapy for bacteremia, adjustment of immunosuppression and inpatient rehabilitation
outcome: GCS improved to 10T within 7.5 h of arrival. Transaminases peaked on day 1 and creatine kinase on day 2; bacteremia needed prolonged antibiotics. Discharged walking on hospital day 42 without neurological sequelae and with no organ dysfunction beyond the rhabdomyolysis and hepatic injury.
teachingPoints: Exertional heat stroke is hyperthermia (typically core temperature above 40 °C) with central nervous system dysfunction during or after exertion in heat; lack of acclimatization is a classic risk factor.
Use rectal (or esophageal) temperature: here the bladder probe read 40.1 °C while the rectal temperature was 42.0 °C, and axillary, oral and tympanic readings are unreliable.

Cool first: aim for a core temperature below 39 °C within about 30 minutes. Cold-water immersion is the gold standard (about 0.15–0.35 °C/min); an ice-water tarp or body bag with oscillation is a practical bridge when no tub is available.
Intubation, IV access and monitoring can be done during immersion; stop active cooling at about 39 °C to avoid overshoot. Antipyretics and dantrolene have no role.
Anticipate rhabdomyolysis and liver injury peaking over 1–2 days, and look for sepsis in high-risk hosts; this patient's blood cultures later grew S. caprae.

questions.q: What is the most important immediate intervention?
options: IV acetaminophen with cooling blankets, then reassess
CT head and lumbar puncture before starting cooling
Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, then evaporative cooling
Immediate whole-body ice-water cooling, aiming for <39 °C within 30 min
questions.explanation: Coma with a rectal temperature of 42 °C after exertion in the heat is exertional heat stroke, and outcome depends on how fast the core temperature falls. Cold-water immersion is the preferred method (Wilderness Medical Society heat illness guidelines); an ice-water tarp or body bag is a practical bridge when no tub is available. Antipyretics and dantrolene do not work, and the work-up for sepsis or CNS infection should run alongside cooling, not before it.

questions.q: Which temperature measurement should guide his cooling?
questions.extra: On arrival: rectal temperature 42.0 °C and bladder temperature 40.1 °C at the same time; axillary temperature during transport 42.0 °C.
options: Tympanic infrared temperature, because it reflects brain temperature
Rectal (or esophageal) temperature from a continuous probe
Axillary temperature, because it is quick and non-invasive
Temporal-artery scan, because it tracks rapid changes best
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature, or esophageal temperature in an intubated patient, is the standard for diagnosing exertional heat stroke and guiding cooling; oral, axillary, tympanic and temporal readings underestimate core temperature, especially in a hot environment or during cooling. Here the bladder probe read almost 2 °C lower than the rectal probe at the same moment.

questions.q: When should active cooling be stopped?
questions.extra: Ice-water body bag cooling under way; rectal temperature falling from 42.0 °C.
options: When the rectal temperature falls to about 38.6–39 °C
When the rectal temperature reaches 37 °C or lower
After a fixed 15 minutes, whatever the temperature
As soon as he shivers or his GCS starts to improve
questions.explanation: Active cooling stops at a core temperature of about 39 °C (38.6–39 °C in expert consensus such as ACSM; here at 38.7 °C) to avoid overshoot hypothermia, with continued monitoring for rebound. A fixed duration or mental status is not a safe endpoint; he reached the target in 39 minutes.

questions.q: Which factor most strongly determines morbidity and mortality in exertional heat stroke?
options: The peak temperature, regardless of how long it lasts
The creatine kinase level on arrival
How long the core temperature stays above about 40 °C
Whether a seizure occurred at the time of collapse
questions.explanation: Outcome tracks the duration of severe hyperthermia, which is why cooling starts at once and cooling rate matters; in a 521-patient series cited by the authors, cooling slower than 0.15 °C/min was associated with deaths and complications that were almost absent with faster cooling. Peak temperature and initial creatine kinase are weaker predictors.

evidence.quote: A 57-year-old male construction worker was brought to the ED via physician-staffed ambulance following collapse at a construction site.
a history of acute myeloid leukemia status post umbilical cord blood transplantation 7 months ago and was maintained on immunosuppressive therapy (prednisolone 5 mg, tacrolimus 0.2 mg)
He had returned to work the previous day without adequate heat acclimatization.

While performing outdoor pipe-cutting work in ambient conditions of 36.0℃ and 65% humidity, the patient experienced dizziness after 90 min of labor and subsequently collapsed with witnessed seizure-like activity
Emergency medical services arrived within 26 min, and prehospital cooling was initiated with cold intravenous fluids (500 mL)
During transport, he presented with Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3 (E1V1M1), blood pressure 72/49 mmHg, heart rate 155 /minute, respiratory rate 30 /minute, and axillary temperature 42.0℃.
On arrival at 10:30, rectal temperature was 42.0℃ and bladder temperature was 40.1℃, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, and heart rate 183 beats/minute.
Physical exam revealed GCS score of 4 (E1V2M1) and marked skin warmth.
Initial laboratory findings showed mild hyponatremia (126 mEq/L), elevated creatine kinase (217 U/L)
transaminitis (aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 244 U/L, alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 145 U/L), and elevated lactate levels (43.0 mg/dL)
No coagulopathy was observed.
The cooling apparatus consisted of a body bag filled with 15 L of tap water and 15 kg of ice cubes, prepared in advance.
Approximately half of the patient’s body was immersed.
implemented continuous oscillation by manually agitating the bag from four corners. Adjunctive cooling measures included ice packs applied to bilateral axillae and groins.
endotracheal intubation was performed while the patient remained immersed in the cooling apparatus, using ketamine and rocuronium
The patient was continuously monitored via defibrillator pads (no arrhythmia), ear-lobe pulse oximetry, and intermittent right upper arm blood pressure
alongside continuous bladder and intermittent rectal temperature monitoring
Simultaneous resuscitation included cold intravenous of acetated Ringer’s solution (total of 2,500 mL during ED stay).
TACO was discontinued at 11:09 when rectal temperature reached 38.7℃, yielding a cooling rate of 0.085℃/minute over 39 min.
After reaching the target temperature, one corner of the body bag was cut to drain the water
Consciousness improved to GCS of 10T (E4VTM6) within 7.5 h of hospital arrival.
peaking of transaminases on hospital day 1 (AST 572 U/L, ALT 358 U/L)
a peak creatine kinase of 2,165 U/L on hospital day 2 consistent with hepatic injury and rhabdomyolysis
Blood cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus caprae with no source.
He was transferred from the ICU on hospital day 5 following overall clinical stabilization, with ongoing antimicrobial therapy.
continued antimicrobial treatment, immunosuppressive regimen adjustment, and inpatient rehabilitation
The hospital course was complicated by bacteremia requiring prolonged antimicrobial therapy.
resulting in discharge on hospital day 42 ambulatory and without neurological sequelae, with no organ dysfunction beyond the rhabdomyolysis and hepatic injury
We present a case of severe EHS successfully treated with immediate body bag-based TACO upon ED arrival
